summary: Records the threats against the Domain Name System that DNSSEC is meant to protect against, something that was never written down while DNSSEC was being developed. It helps judge whether DNSSEC actually meets its goals and what it leaves unaddressed.

eli5.summary: Before putting locks on a house, you list the ways burglars could get in. This document lists the ways bad guys can trick the internet's phone book.

questions: what is a name chaining attack
subtitle: The list of attacks on DNS that DNSSEC was meant to defend against, written down a decade late.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC was developed for about a decade without the IETF writing down the threats it was meant to stop, so it was hard to judge whether it met its goals.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC catalogs the known threats to DNS (packet interception, ID guessing, name chaining, a betraying trusted server, denial of service, missing-name and wildcard problems) and says for each how far DNSSEC helps.
tldr.outcome: The authors conclude DNSSEC solves a set of problems that need solving and is worth deploying, while admitting it has weaknesses of its own and does not stop denial of service.

facts.label: Services DNSSEC targets
facts.value: Data integrity and data origin authentication

today: RFC 3833 is an Informational document, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the threat model that DNSSEC was measured against as of August 2004.

sections.title: Background and Scope
sections.content:
The earliest organized DNSSEC work was a design team meeting at the 28th IETF meeting in Houston in November 1993. That meeting decided that "DNS data is public", so protecting against data disclosure was out of scope, and so was authenticating clients and servers for access control. The wanted security services were data integrity and data origin authentication, and a digital signature mechanism would provide them. Backward compatibility with insecure DNS was an explicit requirement.

The RFC assumes the reader already knows DNS and DNSSEC. It uses the term "DNSSEC" for the core hierarchical public key and signature mechanism, and treats TKEY and TSIG as separate channel security mechanisms.
sections.eli5: The planners decided the phone book is public, so the goal is not hiding what is in it, only making sure the entries are real and unchanged.

sections.title: Interception, Guessing and Betrayal
sections.content:
Packet interception covers eavesdropping and spoofed answers that beat the real one back to the resolver. DNS usually sends a whole query or response in one unsigned, unencrypted UDP packet, which makes this easy for anyone on a shared or transit network. Signing with TSIG or IPsec would be costly and would only give a hop-by-hop check, not end-to-end integrity between the zone administrator and the application. DNSSEC gives that end-to-end check. Note that DNSSEC does not protect the DNS message header.

ID guessing and query prediction works because the DNS ID is only 16 bits and the server port is well known, leaving about 2**32 combinations of ID and client port, and often far fewer when the port is fixed or predictable. A resolver that checks DNSSEC signatures can detect the forged response.

Betrayal by a trusted server is the case where a stub resolver relies on a recursive server, often supplied by the ISP via DHCP or PPP, that gives wrong answers by accident or design. The defense is the same: check DNSSEC signatures yourself, or authenticate the server with TSIG. TSIG alone does not make a server trustworthy. The RFC concludes a properly paranoid resolver must always do its own signature checking, even a stub resolver, and for that it needs independent knowledge of the DNSSEC public keys, usually the root zone key.
sections.eli5: A cheater can shout a fake answer faster than the real one, guess the secret numbers on a question, or be the helper you asked in the first place. Checking the answer's signature yourself catches the fake.

sections.title: Name Chaining and Authenticated Denial
sections.content:
Name chaining is the most DNS-specific threat. It is a kind of cache poisoning that uses resource records whose data includes a DNS name. CNAME, NS and DNAME are the worst, since they can redirect a query to a place the attacker chooses. MX and SRV are less dangerous, and even A and AAAA records can matter because of the IN-ADDR.ARPA and IP6.ARPA trees. An attacker can provoke the query easily, for example with a 1x1-pixel "web bug" in an HTML mail. DNSSEC should defend against most of these, because signatures show whether the data was inserted by the delegated authority. Glue records are not covered by signatures, but a resolver can fetch the signed authoritative copy and check that.

Authenticated denial of domain names addresses an attacker removing records from a response. Missing MX and SRV records fall back to A records, so removal is a real threat. DNSSEC can prove which names exist in a zone and which record types exist at them.

Wildcards need two things: proof the wildcard record exists, and proof that no record exists that would make the wildcard irrelevant. This makes wildcards depend on authenticated denial.
sections.eli5: A liar can slip in a note saying "go ask my friend instead". Signatures show who really wrote each note, and a signed "nothing here" stops someone from erasing a real entry.

sections.title: Denial of Service and DNSSEC Weaknesses
sections.content:
DNSSEC does not help against denial of service, and can make it worse for resolvers that check signatures, since validation adds processing and sometimes more messages. DNS servers can also be used as amplifiers because responses are longer than queries, and DNSSEC makes responses bigger still.

Section 3 lists weaknesses of DNSSEC itself. It is complex, with tricky edge cases at zone cuts, and simple zone errors or expired keys can cause serious problems. Validation increases resolver workload and delay. Its trust model is almost totally hierarchical, so a compromise of any zone between the root and a target name can damage protection. Root key rollover was not adequately specified. Signatures use absolute time, so validating resolvers and signers need loosely synchronized clocks, and an attacker who changes a resolver's clock could make it accept expired signatures. Wildcards complicate authenticated denial.
sections.eli5: The new lock does not stop a crowd from jamming the door, and it adds extra paperwork, a clock to keep right and a chain of trust that can break at any link.

sections.title: Future Work and Conclusion
sections.content:
The RFC points to areas needing study. Dynamic update of a secure zone needs a zone-signing key to be available, either to the updating client or online at the name server, which is a security risk, and the access control for update is coarse-grained. Zone replication: DNSSEC provides object security for query answers, but not for whole zones, because zones contain unsigned NS records and glue at delegation points. TSIG on zone transfers gives channel security only, a hop-by-hop matter between name server operators.

The conclusion is short: DNSSEC does appear to solve a set of problems that need to be solved, and is worth deploying. The security considerations section adds that DNSSEC helps with some, but not all, of the known threats to DNS.
sections.eli5: There are still gaps, like safely changing the phone book while it is signed. But the lock is worth installing.
